modalities.name: Clean Slate Pickup
modalities.tagline: A captainless game where every point starts from zero.
modalities.whatItIs: Clean Slate Pickup is a drop-in team game, such as Ultimate, in which nothing from the past is allowed to count. Teams are redrawn before every point, no score is carried over and nobody becomes known as the best or worst player. Ideal Parent Figure work builds an imagined past; this point on the map has no past at all, only the point being played.
modalities.coreIdea: When teams, scores and reputations reset every point, all that is left is the play happening right now, run entirely by the players.
modalities.whatYouDo: Twelve to twenty players meet at a park for about 90 minutes, warm up together, then draw colored bibs from a bag before each point to form new teams. Each point is played flat out and then let go: no tally, no stats, no captains and no coach, and calls are settled by the two players involved. The session ends with a short circle where people name one moment they enjoyed, not who won.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel boxed in by labels, rankings or their own history, and anyone who wants a fast, sociable game with no pecking order.
modalities.cautions: Full-speed sprinting and cutting bring leg injuries and a risk of head knocks, so warm up, build fitness gradually, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea and is not a substitute for therapy for attachment or relationship difficulties.
modalities.tweet: Fresh concept: Clean Slate Pickup. A drop-in game where teams are redrawn every point, nobody keeps score and no one has a reputation, so every point starts from zero. No labels, no rankings, no history. Just the point you're playing.

modalities.name: Turncoat Whistle
modalities.tagline: Mid-game, a whistle sends you to play for the other side.
modalities.whatItIs: Turncoat Whistle is a full-speed team game in which a whistle, blown at random every few minutes, sends two named players across to the other team, where they must play just as hard for their former opponents. Nobody stays on one side for long, so 'us' and 'them' keep changing.
modalities.coreIdea: Switching sides mid-game may loosen rigid us-and-them thinking and show that you can commit fully to whoever you are with right now.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two teams of seven play a 60-minute disc game, and a timekeeper with the player list blows the whistle every four to seven minutes and calls two names, one from each side. Those two swap bibs on the spot and play on, and points stay with the team, not the player. At the end, players say which switch felt strangest and why.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who get locked into rivalries or sides at work or online, and anyone curious how loyalty feels when it keeps moving.
modalities.cautions: Full-speed play brings risks of strains, collisions and head knocks, so warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, and the swaps should stay playful, never a test of anyone's commitment.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Turncoat Whistle. A full-speed team game where every few minutes a whistle sends two players to the other side, and they have to play their hearts out for the rivals they were just marking. A weekly workout in not getting stuck on one side.

modalities.name: Rule Jam Games
modalities.tagline: A nonstop running game whose rules are voted in and out.
modalities.whatItIs: Rule Jam Games is a fast running game with no fixed rulebook: players start from a basic disc or ball game and vote new rules in and out as they play. Sitting as far as it can from structured, agenda-driven therapy such as CBT, it has no plan, no score kept past each round and no goal of getting better. One rule never changes: whatever is voted in has to keep everyone running.
modalities.coreIdea: Playing hard under rules you did not choose, and that may change again in ten minutes, is meant to be practice in going along with change without needing a plan.
modalities.whatYouDo: A group of 10 to 20 meets on a field for an hour of nonstop play with a few discs, balls and cones. Every ten minutes anyone can propose a rule, such as 'throws must be backhand' or 'two discs at once', and a show of hands decides it, so most players end up running under rules they voted against. Nobody keeps score beyond the current round.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find sport too rigid or get unsettled when plans change, and who want to practice change somewhere it is only a game.
modalities.cautions: Constant running and improvised rules can lead to collisions, falls and strains, so keep two rules fixed (no contact, no diving), warm up, stop playing after any knock to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, not a form of therapy.
modalities.tweet: An idea for grown-ups who miss real play: Rule Jam Games. Start with a disc, vote a new rule in or out every ten minutes and keep running, even under rules you voted against. No plan, no stats, just a game that keeps changing under your feet.

modalities.name: Silent Signal Matches
modalities.tagline: Full-speed team games played without a single spoken word.
modalities.whatItIs: Silent Signal Matches are full-speed team games, such as Ultimate, played under one extra rule: nobody speaks. Teammates coordinate through eye contact, pointing, timing and a handful of agreed hand signs, and even disputed calls are settled in signs. ACT works through words, metaphors and talk about values; this keeps all of the connection and none of the language.
modalities.coreIdea: Taking words out of the game means teamwork has to happen through the eyes and body, so people connect and cooperate without explaining themselves.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before a 90-minute session, the group spends ten minutes learning six hand signs, for example for 'I'm open', 'foul' and 'replay the point'. Games are then played at full speed in total silence, with a short spoken break at halftime to adjust the signs. The session ends with players sharing, out loud this time, what they noticed about teammates when nobody could talk.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find talking draining or feel they always over-explain, and teams that want sharper teamwork without words.
modalities.cautions: Without shouted warnings collisions are more likely, so play no-contact, keep a whistle or a loud clap for emergencies, warm up properly, stop playing after any knock to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested concept, and some people find enforced silence uncomfortable, so it should stay optional.
modalities.tweet: New idea: Silent Signal Matches. A full-speed team game where nobody says a word. You read eyes, point, time your cuts and settle calls with hand signs. Connection through movement, with all the talking taken out. 🤫

modalities.name: No Sorry Game
modalities.tagline: Mistakes allowed, apologies banned: the team just says 'next'.
modalities.whatItIs: No Sorry Game is a hard, fast team game with one banned word: sorry. After a drop, a wild throw or a missed block, players may not apologize or explain, and the whole team simply says 'next' and plays on. Coherence Therapy searches for the hidden reason behind a reaction; this goes the other way, with no reasons, no stories and no post-mortems, only the following point.
modalities.coreIdea: Banning apologies and explanations for mistakes is meant to make errors ordinary, so attention goes back to the game instead of to blame.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two teams of seven play for 60 to 90 minutes with the usual rules plus the ban, and anyone who says sorry or starts explaining a mistake jogs once around a cone, laughter allowed. Teammates answer every error with a clap and 'next'. In the closing circle, each player names one mistake they let go of quickly.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who apologize all the time, replay their mistakes or brace for blame, and teams whose mood sinks after errors.
modalities.cautions: Fast play brings risks of strains, collisions and head knocks, so warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, and the ban covers mistakes only: a real injury or foul still deserves a word of care.
modalities.tweet: Experimental team game: No Sorry Game. Drop the disc, throw it away, miss the block, and you're not allowed to apologize or explain. Your team just claps and says 'next'. Ninety minutes of making mistakes ordinary, at full speed.

modalities.name: All Hands Scoring
modalities.tagline: No point counts until every player on the team has scored.
modalities.whatItIs: All Hands Scoring is a team game with one scoring rule: a team's points count only once every player on it has scored at least once, and until then they are tallied but frozen. Strong players cannot carry the game alone, so the whole team talks, plans and shouts to get the disc to whoever has not scored yet.
modalities.coreIdea: When no point counts until everyone has scored, attention may turn to including the person who is usually left out, and being included stops depending on skill.
modalities.whatYouDo: Mixed teams of seven play a 75-minute game, and a sideline volunteer ticks a box for each player the first time they score. Once all seven boxes are ticked, the team's frozen points unlock and the boxes reset for another round. Teams keep calling out the names of who still needs a score, so the talk on the field never stops.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who usually feel sidelined in sport, and strong players who want to practice making room for others.
modalities.cautions: Full-speed play brings risks of strains, collisions and head knocks, so warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, and the attention on players who have not scored yet should stay friendly, never mocking.
modalities.tweet: What if your team's goals only counted once every single player had scored? All Hands Scoring turns a game into a loud, joint effort to get the disc to whoever usually gets left out. Strong players can't carry it alone.

modalities.name: Yes First Game
modalities.tagline: Any teammate calls a play; everyone says yes and goes.
modalities.whatItIs: Yes First Game brings an improv theater rule onto a sports field: when any teammate calls a play, everyone says yes and commits at once, with no debate and no better idea. Calls can be odd, such as 'everyone stack left' or 'long throw now', and the fun is in going all in together.
modalities.coreIdea: Committing fully and immediately to someone else's idea may loosen the habit of judging, hesitating and holding back.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two teams of seven play for an hour, and before each point any player may shout one call that the whole team then follows at full speed. Nobody may argue with a call, only build on it ('yes, and I'll go deep'). After the game, players share the silliest call that worked.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who hesitate, overthink or always have a better idea, and teams that want more trust and energy.
modalities.cautions: Sudden all-in plays raise the risk of collisions, strains and head knocks, so warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, and anyone may still refuse a call that feels unsafe.
modalities.tweet: Idea: Yes First Game. Any teammate can call a play, however odd, and everyone says yes and goes all in, instantly. No debate, only 'yes, and'. An improv rule taken onto a sports field, as practice in trusting someone else's idea.

modalities.name: Wristband Dares
modalities.tagline: A small dare taped to your wrist, done mid-game.
modalities.whatItIs: Wristband Dares turns a weekly team game into a place to rehearse small acts of nerve: each player writes one personal dare on tape around their wrist, such as asking loudly for the disc five times or making a call they would normally swallow. A buddy on the team quietly checks it off.
modalities.coreIdea: Small, self-chosen dares inside a fast game may make courage something you practice with friends around rather than something you wait to feel.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before a 90-minute game, everyone picks a dare from a shared list or writes their own, tapes it on and tells one buddy. During play the buddy notices when it happens and gives a thumbs up, and at the end each player says whether they did it and how it felt. Dares grow a little bolder week by week, chosen only by the player.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who go quiet in groups, swallow their opinions or never ask for what they want, and who would rather practice that in a game than in a meeting.
modalities.cautions: Full-speed play brings risks of strains, collisions and head knocks, so warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, and no dare should put anyone's body or dignity at risk.
modalities.tweet: Proposal: Wristband Dares. Before the game, tape one small dare to your wrist (ask for the disc five times, make the call you usually swallow) and a teammate quietly checks it off. Courage practice dressed up as a pickup game.

modalities.name: Three-Step Stop
modalities.tagline: At full speed, a random whistle means: stop, breathe, go.
modalities.whatItIs: Three-Step Stop is a full-speed team game in which a whistle, blown at random, means every player brings themselves to a stop within three steps, holds still for one slow breath and then plays on. Do Nothing meditation drops all control; this sits at the opposite pole, practicing the most deliberate control there is, which is stopping yourself at the height of excitement. Between whistles the game is played hard and fast.
modalities.coreIdea: Bringing yourself to a calm stop in the middle of maximal excitement, again and again, is meant to be practice in pausing when you are fired up.
modalities.whatYouDo: Teams of seven play a 60-minute game, and a sideline volunteer blows the whistle six to ten times at random moments. On each whistle every player slows to a stop over three steps, breathes out slowly once, and play resumes from where the disc is. At the end, players say which stop was hardest.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who act on impulse when wound up or say things in the heat of the moment, and anyone who wants practice switching from full speed to calm.
modalities.cautions: Sudden stops strain knees and ankles, so the rule is to slow down over three steps, never to freeze mid-stride; warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: what if a game could stop you mid-sprint? Three-Step Stop is a hard, fast team game where a random whistle means slow to a stop in three steps, one long breath out, play on. Practice in pausing when you're fired up.

modalities.name: Three Disc Mayhem
modalities.tagline: A team game with three discs in play at once.
modalities.whatItIs: Three Disc Mayhem is a loose, chaotic team game played with three discs live at the same time, so nobody can see or manage everything that is happening. Metta and jhana meditation settle attention on one warm inner feeling; here attention is flung outward across a whole field, with no hope of total control. Rules are minimal and the mood is playful.
modalities.coreIdea: With too much going on for anyone to track, players may learn to stop trying to control the whole game and trust teammates to cover what they cannot see.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two teams of seven play 10-minute rounds on a normal field, and each team can score with any of the three discs, while a score with one disc does not stop the others. Players call out names constantly so that passes can find them, and nobody tracks the total score. A session lasts about an hour, with short breaks between rounds.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel they must keep track of everything, at work or at home, and anyone who loves noisy, unpredictable games.
modalities.cautions: With several discs flying, the risk of being hit or colliding goes up, so use soft discs, play no-contact, keep your eyes up, stop playing after any knock to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, and the chaos may feel overwhelming to some players.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: what if a team game had three discs in play at once? In Three Disc Mayhem there's far too much to track, so you stop trying to control everything and trust your teammates with what you can't see.

modalities.name: Feelings on the Field
modalities.tagline: Shout a feeling in one word mid-play; a teammate answers 'heard'.
modalities.whatItIs: Feelings on the Field is a fast team game in which players call out their feelings as they happen, in one word ('frustrated!', 'buzzing!', 'nervous!'), and the nearest teammate answers 'heard'. Vipassana watches inner states silently and without reacting. Here they are named out loud, in company, in the middle of play.
modalities.coreIdea: Naming a feeling the moment it arrives, and having someone simply acknowledge it, may make feelings easier to say in everyday life too.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before a 75-minute game, the group agrees on a short list of feeling words and on 'heard' as the only reply allowed, with no advice and no teasing. During play anyone can call a word at any time, and at halftime each player says which feeling came up most. The game ends with a circle of one word each.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who struggle to say what they feel, and teams that want an honest, warm atmosphere.
modalities.cautions: Fast play brings risks of strains, collisions and head knocks, so warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, and calling feelings must stay optional, since some people will not want to share.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Feelings on the Field. Mid-game, shout how you feel in one word ('frustrated!', 'buzzing!') and the nearest teammate answers 'heard'. No advice, no teasing, then play on. Saying what you feel, at full speed and in company.

modalities.name: Slow Motion Rounds
modalities.tagline: Every other round played in dramatic, narrated slow motion.
modalities.whatItIs: Slow Motion Rounds is a gentle, silly team game in which every other round is played in exaggerated slow motion, like a film replay, while someone on the sideline narrates it like a nature documentary. The other rounds are played at an easy jog, so the effort stays moderate throughout. HIIT is about all-out bursts; this is about laughing at yourself together.
modalities.coreIdea: Moving absurdly slowly in front of others, with everyone doing the same, is meant to dissolve self-consciousness and turn being watched into shared fun.
modalities.whatYouDo: Mixed groups of 10 to 16 play six 8-minute rounds over an hour, alternating easy jogging rounds with slow-motion rounds in which throws, catches and celebrations are acted out at a crawl. Anyone can join whatever their fitness, and nobody keeps score in slow-motion rounds. The session ends with a vote for the most dramatic slow-motion moment.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel self-conscious moving in front of others, newcomers to sport, and anyone who wants a laugh more than a workout.
modalities.cautions: Slow, exaggerated moves can still strain muscles or cause falls, so keep them within a comfortable range, never dive, stop playing after any knock to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, and the jokes should be about the game, never about anyone's body.
modalities.tweet: Picture this: a team game where every other round is played in dramatic slow motion while someone narrates it like a nature documentary. Slow Motion Rounds is a new idea for anyone who feels self-conscious moving in front of people. 🐢

modalities.name: Moving End Zones
modalities.tagline: Every three minutes, the place you are attacking moves.
modalities.whatItIs: Moving End Zones is a team game in which the field keeps changing: every three minutes a timer sounds and two volunteers move the end-zone cones to a new spot, so the target shifts while you play. The rules stay fixed, so the only thing that changes is where the goal is.
modalities.coreIdea: Having the goal move without warning, while the rules hold, offers practice in re-orienting quickly instead of clinging to the old plan.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two teams of seven play for an hour on a large field marked with spare cones, and on each timer the end zones move to one of six marked positions, drawn by card. Teams get ten seconds to re-orient and then play on from where the disc is. After the game, players talk about what they did when the goal moved.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are thrown by sudden change at work or at home, and teams that want more adaptable play.
modalities.cautions: Sudden changes of direction strain knees and ankles and raise the risk of collisions, so warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: New idea: Moving End Zones. Every three minutes the cones move and the place you're attacking is suddenly somewhere else. Same rules, shifting ground. A team game for practicing what to do when the goal moves halfway through.

modalities.name: Tethered Pairs
modalities.tagline: Play the whole game within arm's reach of a partner.
modalities.whatItIs: Tethered Pairs is a team game in which every player is paired with a teammate and must stay within arm's reach of them all game, cutting, defending and catching as a pair. Strength training builds individual force through counted sets; this asks you to give up solo speed and move at the pace of another body. There is no rope, only an agreement, and a lot of laughing.
modalities.coreIdea: Staying in step with a partner at speed is meant to train attunement: noticing another person's pace and intentions and adjusting to them.
modalities.whatYouDo: Teams of eight, in four pairs, play a 60-minute disc game, and a pair that drifts more than arm's length apart gives the disc away. Pairs swap partners every 15 minutes, so each player tunes in to four different people. The session ends with partners telling each other one thing they noticed about how the other moves.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who tend to run ahead of others or get lost in their own pace, and anyone who wants to feel closely in sync with someone.
modalities.cautions: Moving as a pair raises the risk of tripping over each other and colliding, so never hold hands or use a rope, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Tethered Pairs. Everyone plays in twos and must stay within arm's reach of their partner all game, cutting, catching and defending as a unit. You give up solo speed and get something else: a feel for someone else's pace.

modalities.name: Marker's Honest Minute
modalities.tagline: Compete hard all game, then swap honest notes with your rival.
modalities.whatItIs: Marker's Honest Minute is a competitive team game that ends in an unusual ritual: you sit down with the opponent you marked most and each of you gives the other one honest observation about their play and one about how they handled calls. The game before it is played hard.
modalities.coreIdea: Swapping honest, specific feedback with someone you just competed against may make giving and hearing criticism feel less threatening.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two teams play a hard 60-minute game in which each player marks the same opponent as much as possible. Afterward each pair sits apart for two minutes each way and follows a card (one thing you did well, one thing you could change, one fair moment I noticed), and the only reply allowed is 'thanks'. Pairs rotate each week.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who dread feedback or avoid conflict, and competitive players who want to compete hard and stay on good terms.
modalities.cautions: Hard competitive play brings risks of strains, collisions and head knocks, so warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, and feedback should stay about play and fairness, never about anyone's body or personality.
modalities.tweet: Concept: Marker's Honest Minute. Play hard against one opponent all game, then sit down together and swap one honest observation each way, answered only with 'thanks'. A new way to practice feedback, with the person who just tried to beat you.

modalities.name: Call for a Sub
modalities.tagline: Shout 'sub' any time, for any reason, and you're out.
modalities.whatItIs: Call for a Sub is a fast, intense team game with one firm rule: any player can call 'sub' at any moment, for any reason or none, and is replaced at once with no questions asked. Qigong regulates the body quietly from the inside, whereas this asks you to notice your own limit while fired up and say it out loud. Fields are small and the play comes in bursts.
modalities.coreIdea: Saying 'I need a break' in the middle of excitement, and seeing it honored instantly, may make it easier to speak up about limits elsewhere.
modalities.whatYouDo: Groups of 12 to 16 play short, intense games with a deep bench, and any call of 'sub' pauses play for the swap. Calling it is applauded, never questioned, and there is no limit on how often anyone calls it. The session closes with players saying whether they called it as soon as they first noticed they needed to.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who push past their limits to keep up, find it hard to ask for rest, or feel they always have to be the one who keeps going.
modalities.cautions: Intense bursts strain the heart, knees and ankles and raise the risk of collisions and head knocks, so build fitness first, warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart problems or high blood pressure. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: New idea: Call for a Sub. A fast, intense team game where anyone can shout 'sub' at any moment, for any reason, and is swapped out instantly to applause. No questions asked. Practice in saying 'I need a break' while everyone else keeps going.

modalities.name: Unison Openers
modalities.tagline: Every session starts with the whole team moving as one.
modalities.whatItIs: Unison Openers start every team session with a short warm-up sequence that the whole squad performs in exact unison, counted out like a drill team, before any play begins. Socializing builds closeness through conversation, and this builds it by moving together, step for step, with no need to talk. The sequence is learned once and refined over a season.
modalities.coreIdea: Some studies link moving in time with others to feeling closer to them, so a shared opening may help a team feel like one group before the first point.
modalities.whatYouDo: The team writes an eight-count sequence of warm-up moves (jogging, high knees, lunges, side shuffles) and learns it together, then performs it in a tight block at the start of every session, ending with one shared shout. A new move is added each month. The rest of the session is ordinary hard training and play.
modalities.whoItsFor: Teams that feel like a collection of individuals, and people who bond more easily by doing than by talking.
modalities.cautions: A shared tempo can push some players too fast, so keep the sequence moderate and build it up gradually, stop playing after any knock to the head during the session and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Speculative idea: Unison Openers. Every team session begins with a warm-up the whole squad performs in exact unison, step for step, ending in one shared shout. Closeness built by moving together rather than by talking.

modalities.name: Win Card Game
modalities.tagline: Each team writes its own definition of winning before kick-off.
modalities.whatItIs: Win Card Game is a timed, structured team game in which each team writes down its own definition of winning before play starts, such as 'everyone throws a goal' or 'we never argue a call'. The result is judged against those words, not just the scoreboard.
modalities.coreIdea: Choosing your own measure of success, and checking it afterward, may loosen the grip of the one measure everybody else uses.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each team has five minutes to agree on two win conditions and write them on a card, which the other team reads aloud. They then play a timed 60-minute game with the score kept as usual, and at the end each team checks its card and declares whether it won on its own terms. Cards are rewritten each week.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who measure themselves only by results, and teams that want to care about how they play as much as about the score.
modalities.cautions: Full-speed play brings risks of strains, collisions and head knocks, so warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Hypothetical game: Win Card Game. Before kick-off, each team writes its own definition of winning ('everyone scores', 'no arguing calls') and is judged by that card as well as the scoreboard. Choosing your own measure of success, then playing for it.

modalities.name: Read Their Plan
modalities.tagline: Guess the other team's secret strategy from how they move.
modalities.whatItIs: Read Their Plan is a team game with a hidden layer: before each half, each team secretly writes a one-line strategy on a card, and during play the other team tries to work it out. A correct guess at the break earns a bonus point. Sensory mindfulness rests on what the senses meet, and this asks players to read minds from movement, thinking hard while running hard.
modalities.coreIdea: Guessing other people's intentions from how they move, and then finding out how often you were wrong, may soften certainty about what others are thinking.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two teams of seven play two 30-minute halves, writing a secret plan card before each, such as 'always throw to the left side'. At halftime and full time, each team gets one guess at the other's card. Afterward players compare what they thought they saw with what was really going on.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who enjoy strategy, and anyone who often assumes they know what others are thinking and would like to test it.
modalities.cautions: Fast play brings risks of strains, collisions and head knocks, so warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Idea: Read Their Plan. Each team secretly writes a one-line strategy, then spends the half trying to guess the other's from how they move, with a bonus point for a correct read. Mind-reading, checked against reality every 30 minutes.

modalities.name: Quiet Ones Call It
modalities.tagline: The quietest players lead; the loudest play in silence.
modalities.whatItIs: Quiet Ones Call It is a team game that flips who gets heard: the players who usually talk least make all the calls, choose the lines and lead the huddles, while the usual loud voices must stay silent. Who counts as quiet or loud is decided by the players themselves, privately, before the game.
modalities.coreIdea: Giving the floor to the quietest voices, and asking the loudest to follow, may let each group feel what the other usually feels.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before a 75-minute game, each player privately rates on a slip how much they usually talk on the field, and a volunteer names the three quietest and three loudest on each team. The quiet three call every play and settle every disputed call, and the loud three play in silence, using only signs. The roles are redrawn every week.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who rarely speak up in groups, people who often take over without meaning to, and teams that want more balanced voices.
modalities.cautions: Fast play brings risks of strains, collisions and head knocks, so warm up, play no-contact, stop playing after any knock to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. It is an untested idea, and anyone who finds being singled out stressful can opt out.
modalities.tweet: What if the quietest players made every call and the loudest had to play in silence? Quiet Ones Call It is an untested team game that flips who gets heard, so each side feels what the other usually feels.

modalities.name: Beat the Sunrise
modalities.tagline: Run hard to a viewpoint to arrive before the sun.
modalities.whatItIs: Beat the Sunrise is a hard, self-led run timed to the dawn: you set out in the half-dark and run to a hill, bridge or rooftop-view spot so as to arrive just before the sun comes up, then watch it rise. The only plan is the sunrise time, and the reward is what you see. Nothing is imagined or remembered here, the opposite end of the line from imagery work such as Ideal Parent Figure therapy: there is the light, and your breathing.
modalities.coreIdea: Racing the sun to a view, and then standing still in front of it, may give a regular dose of awe, the feeling of being small in front of something large, which many people rarely make room for.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once or twice a week you check the sunrise time, choose a viewpoint 20 to 40 minutes away and set off early enough to arrive with a few minutes to spare, running hard on the final climb. At the top you stop, catch your breath and watch the light change for five minutes without your phone out. Then you jog home easily.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose days feel small, rushed or the same, and anyone who wants their run to end at something worth seeing.
modalities.cautions: Running in the half-dark brings risks from traffic, uneven ground and cold, so wear a headlamp and reflective clothing, choose safe, familiar routes, tell someone where you are going, build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, not a substitute for professional care.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Beat the Sunrise. Check the sunrise time, pick a viewpoint, then run hard to get there before the sun does. Stand still, phone away, and watch the light come up. A weekly dose of awe, earned with your legs. 🌅

modalities.name: Promise Mile
modalities.tagline: One small, exact promise to yourself on every run, kept.
modalities.whatItIs: Promise Mile is a running practice built on keeping your word to yourself: before one hard stretch of each run you make a single, exact promise, such as 'no walking until the bridge', and then you keep it or note honestly that you did not. Here one clear promise is made and kept, with no negotiating mid-run.
modalities.coreIdea: Making small, exact promises to yourself and keeping them is meant to build self-trust: the sense that when you say you will do something, you do.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you run for 30 to 45 minutes, and before the hard section you say your promise out loud, keeping it small enough to be realistic. Afterward you mark a calendar with a tick for kept or a circle for not kept, and add no other comment. Promises grow only when most of the recent ones were kept.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who often break promises to themselves, or who no longer believe their own plans.
modalities.cautions: A promise must never override pain, dizziness or illness, so build up gradually, stop when your body says so and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, and a circle on the calendar is information, not a failure.
modalities.tweet: Idea: Promise Mile. Before one hard stretch of your run, make one small, exact promise out loud ('no walking until the bridge') and keep it. Tick or circle on the calendar, no comment. Rebuilding self-trust one kept promise at a time.

modalities.name: Run It Wrong
modalities.tagline: A hard run where the only rule is not doing it right.
modalities.whatItIs: Run It Wrong is a hard run with no right way to do it: no form cues, no target pace, no route and no judging, and if you want to flap your arms, zigzag or sprint then skip, you do. Of every point on this line it lies furthest from structured, correct-your-thinking therapy such as CBT. The effort is real; the rules are not.
modalities.coreIdea: Running deliberately without doing it right may loosen the grip of perfectionism, since the only way to fail is to try to do it well.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once or twice a week you run for 20 to 40 minutes on a safe, quiet path or field, as hard as feels good and in whatever style takes you. Whenever you catch yourself correcting your form or checking your pace, you do something sillier instead. Afterward you note one thing you did 'badly' and enjoyed.
modalities.whoItsFor: Perfectionists, people who feel they must do everything properly, and runners for whom running has become a chore of getting it right.
modalities.cautions: Wild changes of pace and direction can strain muscles and joints, so warm up, choose even ground, build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Experimental run: Run It Wrong. No form, no pace, no route. Zigzag, flap your arms, sprint then skip, and the only way to fail is to try to do it well. A hard run for perfectionists who are tired of doing everything properly.

modalities.name: Turnaround Commitment
modalities.tagline: At the halfway point, commit to one thing; do it back home.
modalities.whatItIs: Turnaround Commitment is an out-and-back run with a decision built into its halfway point: when you turn around, you commit out loud to one concrete action for the rest of the day and do it within an hour of getting home. ACT teaches making room for difficult feelings, and this point, on the far side of running from it, uses a run's energy to change something instead. The action is small and specific, such as sending one email or booking one appointment.
modalities.coreIdea: Tying the turnaround in a run to a commitment in your day may make it easier to get from intending to doing while you still have the energy.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before you go, you name a few things you have been putting off. You run out hard for 15 to 25 minutes, and at the turnaround you pick one, say it aloud and run home steadily. Within an hour of finishing, you do it and tick it off.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who put things off, feel stuck, or have plenty of good intentions but little follow-through.
modalities.cautions: Hard running carries injury and heart strain risks, so build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, and if low mood makes even small actions feel impossible, talk to a doctor or therapist.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Turnaround Commitment. Run out hard, and at the turnaround say out loud one small thing you've been putting off. Run home, then do it within the hour. Using a run's energy to get from intending to doing.

modalities.name: Same Loop Again
modalities.tagline: One short loop, run again and again, until only rhythm remains.
modalities.whatItIs: Same Loop Again is a deliberately monotonous running practice: you run one short loop over and over for the whole session. Coherence Therapy digs for meaning in what you feel, but on a loop with nothing new to see or figure out, there is nothing to interpret. Attention settles instead on rhythm, breath and effort.
modalities.coreIdea: When the route offers nothing new, there is nothing left to interpret, and the run becomes pure repetition and rhythm.
modalities.whatYouDo: You pick a safe loop of 400 meters to 1 kilometer, such as a track or a park path, and run it again and again for 30 to 60 minutes at a hard, steady effort. You do not count laps or check splits, and when your mind drifts to the boredom you return to the sound of your breath and footsteps. Once a week is enough.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who overanalyze, who want a simple practice with no decisions, or who are curious what happens when boredom is allowed.
modalities.cautions: Running the same loop, especially on a track, loads the same tissues over and over, so change direction every few laps, build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea and the boredom is part of it, but stop if it feels distressing rather than dull.
modalities.tweet: What happens if you run the same short loop for 45 minutes? Same Loop Again strips away scenery, decisions and novelty until only rhythm, breath and effort are left. A new practice for overthinkers who want something simple.

modalities.name: Forecast Then Run
modalities.tagline: Predict how you'll feel afterward, run, then check the forecast.
modalities.whatItIs: Forecast Then Run is a running practice built around a prediction: before each run you write down how you expect to feel afterward, from 1 to 10, and after it you write how you actually feel. TRE lets the body release tension without words or thought, while this adds a small piece of deliberate thinking, testing your forecasts against what really happens. The runs themselves are hard and steady.
modalities.coreIdea: People often misjudge how they will feel after exercise, and checking your forecasts against reality may make your gloomier predictions about yourself feel less certain.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before three runs a week of 25 to 45 minutes, you note one number for how you expect to feel afterward and one word for why. After cooling down you write the real number. After a month you look at how far off your forecasts were, and in which direction.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose predictions about their own feelings keep them on the sofa, and anyone curious how accurate those predictions are.
modalities.cautions: Hard running carries injury and heart strain risks, so build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, and forecasts that are always bleak are worth mentioning to a doctor or therapist.
modalities.tweet: Idea worth testing: Forecast Then Run. Before each run, write down how you expect to feel afterward, 1 to 10. After, write the real number. A month of that shows how good (or bad) your forecasts about yourself really are.

modalities.name: Speech on the Move
modalities.tagline: Rehearse the words you dread, out loud, with a racing heart.
modalities.whatItIs: Speech on the Move uses a hard, steady run to rehearse difficult words: the conversation you dread, the request you keep postponing or the talk you have to give, spoken out loud while your heart is pounding. Focusing waits in quiet for a felt sense to find its words. Here the words are already chosen, and they get practiced under pressure.
modalities.coreIdea: Practicing hard words while the body is already activated may make the real conversation feel more familiar when your heart starts racing.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before the run you write down three or four sentences you need to say, then run for 25 to 40 minutes on a quiet route, saying them aloud at different points, especially near the top of climbs. You adjust the words until they feel natural even when you are out of breath. Afterward you note which sentence still feels hardest.
modalities.whoItsFor: People with a hard conversation, interview or speech coming up, and anyone whose voice disappears when they are nervous.
modalities.cautions: Talking while running hard can leave you breathless or dizzy, so ease off when needed, run where you are comfortable speaking aloud, build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: New idea: Speech on the Move. Rehearse the conversation you dread out loud while running hard, so you practice the words with a racing heart. When the real moment comes and your pulse jumps, the sentences will have been there before.

modalities.name: Run As If
modalities.tagline: Each run, play the person you are trying to become.
modalities.whatItIs: Run As If is a running practice of trying on an identity: for each run you choose one quality of the person you are working toward, such as 'someone who finishes things' or 'someone calm under pressure', and run the whole session as that person would. The effort is hard and the role is played seriously.
modalities.coreIdea: Acting as the person you want to become, for one contained hour, may make that person feel less like a fantasy and more like a habit.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before three runs a week of 30 to 50 minutes, you write one line: 'Today I run as someone who...'. During the run you make your choices about pace, hills, posture and the hard part as that person would, and afterward you note one moment when it felt real. You keep the same quality for a few weeks before changing it.
modalities.whoItsFor: People working on a change in how they see themselves, and runners who want each run to rehearse something beyond fitness.
modalities.cautions: Hard efforts strain the heart and muscles, so build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, and the chosen quality should be kind and realistic, never a stick to beat yourself with.
modalities.tweet: Proposed practice: Run As If. Before each run, write 'Today I run as someone who...' (finishes things, stays calm, doesn't quit on hills) and play that person for the whole run. Rehearsing the self you're working toward, one run at a time.

modalities.name: Scripted Minute Run
modalities.tagline: Write tomorrow's run minute by minute, then just follow it.
modalities.whatItIs: Scripted Minute Run is a run decided entirely in advance: the evening before, you write a minute-by-minute script (route, pace, where to push and where to ease), and the next day you simply follow it. Do Nothing meditation lets everything happen without control; this sits at the opposite pole, where every choice has been made and nothing is left to decide. It is meant for days when the mind is already full of decisions.
modalities.coreIdea: Following a script you wrote yourself may give an overloaded mind a rare hour with nothing to decide.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each evening before a run day, you write a 30 to 45 minute script on a card, for example 'minutes 1 to 5 easy to the gate, 6 to 20 hard along the river, turn at the bench'. The next day you follow it exactly, checking nothing but the card and a watch. Afterward you note whether following was easier than deciding.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who make decisions all day, such as managers, carers and parents, and anyone whose head is too busy to plan a run on the spot.
modalities.cautions: A script must never override pain, traffic or bad weather, so stop or change course when you need to, build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, and if needing everything scripted starts to feel rigid or anxious, ease off.
modalities.tweet: Concept: Scripted Minute Run. The night before, write the whole run minute by minute (route, pace, where to push). Next day, just follow the card. One hour with zero decisions, for minds that spend all day deciding.

modalities.name: Panorama Pace
modalities.tagline: When effort narrows your focus, widen it to the whole scene.
modalities.whatItIs: Panorama Pace is a running practice of wide attention under strain: whenever effort narrows your focus onto the pain or a thought, you deliberately soften your gaze until you can see the whole scene again, edges included. Metta and jhana gather attention onto one inner feeling, whereas here it stays spread across the world while you work hard. Structure is minimal.
modalities.coreIdea: Keeping your view wide during hard effort may stop discomfort from shrinking your whole world down to the next few steps.
modalities.whatYouDo: On a familiar, safe route you run for 30 to 45 minutes at a hard, steady effort while softening your gaze, so that you notice movement and color at the edges of your vision. Whenever attention narrows onto the effort or a thought, you widen it again to the whole scene. Open parks, beaches and riverside paths work best.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose attention narrows under stress, and runners who want to stay connected to where they are when it gets hard.
modalities.cautions: A wide gaze must never replace watching your footing and traffic, so use safe, familiar routes, build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, not a substitute for professional care.
modalities.tweet: What if you ran with your attention as wide as the sky? Panorama Pace is a new practice: hard, steady running with a soft gaze that takes in the whole scene, widening again whenever your focus shrinks, so a hard stretch doesn't shrink your world.

modalities.name: Stretch the Good Moment
modalities.tagline: On a hard run, catch each good moment and make it last.
modalities.whatItIs: Stretch the Good Moment is a running practice of savoring: whenever something good shows up during a hard run, such as a cool breeze, a sudden easy stride or the view at the top, you slow your attention down and make it last. Vipassana watches every experience arise and pass with the same calm. This one picks out the good ones and leans in.
modalities.coreIdea: Deliberately lingering on good moments during effort may help them register more fully, for minds that tend to skip past the good and dwell on the hard.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you run for 30 to 45 minutes at a hard, steady effort, and each time a good moment appears you hold it for 10 to 20 seconds: you name it silently, notice where you feel it and let a smile happen if it comes. You aim for five such moments per run. Afterward you write down the best one.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose attention goes straight to what is wrong, and runners who finish every run remembering only the hard parts.
modalities.cautions: Hard running carries injury and heart strain risks, so build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, and it is not a way to push hard feelings away, which are allowed too.
modalities.tweet: Fresh concept: Stretch the Good Moment. On a hard run, whenever something good shows up (a breeze, an easy stride, the view at the top), hold it for 20 seconds and let it land. Five a run. Teaching a busy mind to notice the good parts too.

modalities.name: Let Them Pass
modalities.tagline: An easy run where everyone overtakes you, and you let them.
modalities.whatItIs: Let Them Pass is an easy, unhurried run on a busy park path, with one rule: whoever comes up behind you, you let them overtake, and you never chase anyone. The pace is conversational and there is no plan. HIIT is about pushing to the limit, and this is about not needing to prove anything.
modalities.coreIdea: Being overtaken again and again, on purpose and without reacting, may loosen the habit of comparing yourself with everyone around you.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once or twice a week you jog for 30 to 60 minutes at an easy pace on a route with plenty of other runners. Each time someone passes you, you notice any urge to speed up, let it go and keep your pace, perhaps with a nod. Afterward you count how many people passed you and how many urges you let go.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who compete with everyone, strangers included, and runners who cannot go easy when others are around.
modalities.cautions: Easy running still loads the legs, so increase time gradually, drink water and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: An idea for the competitive: Let Them Pass. An easy run on a busy path where everyone who comes up behind you gets to overtake, and you never chase. Notice the urge to speed up, let it go, keep your pace. Proving nothing, on purpose.

modalities.name: No Task Miles
modalities.tagline: A long solo run with no task for your mind at all.
modalities.whatItIs: No Task Miles is a long, solitary, steady run with no job for the mind: no question to solve, no plan, no podcast and no mindfulness technique. Thoughts can wander anywhere, daydreams included, and nothing has to come of them. It is about as far from team sport as running gets, alone, quiet and inward.
modalities.coreIdea: Giving a busy mind a regular hour with nothing to do and no one to answer to may feel like rest, even while the body works.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week you run for 45 to 75 minutes at a steady, comfortable effort on a familiar, safe route, without headphones and with your phone set to emergencies only. If you notice yourself planning or problem-solving, you let it drift rather than chase it. Nothing is written down afterward.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose minds are always on duty at work or at home, and anyone who is never alone with their own thoughts.
modalities.cautions: Running alone and lost in thought carries safety risks, so use safe, familiar routes, tell someone your route and return time, avoid isolated places after dark, build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, and if wandering thoughts keep turning dark, talk to someone you trust or a professional.
modalities.tweet: New idea: No Task Miles. A long solo run with no task for your mind at all. No podcast, no question to solve, no technique, nothing written afterward. Daydreams allowed. One hour a week when your head is off the clock.

modalities.name: Stop for Anything
modalities.tagline: Stop for anything interesting; count stops, not kilometers.
modalities.whatItIs: Stop for Anything is a loose, playful run in which you must stop for anything that catches your interest: a dog, a strange door, a bird, a view. Instead of distance or pace, you count the stops.
modalities.coreIdea: Letting curiosity interrupt the plan, again and again, may shift attention from achieving to noticing.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once or twice a week you run for 30 to 50 minutes at a moderate pace, and whenever something interests you, you stop, look for as long as you like and then run on. There is no route and no target. At the end you note your stop count and the most interesting thing you saw.
modalities.whoItsFor: People always rushing toward the next goal, and runners who have stopped seeing where they run.
modalities.cautions: Stopping and starting is easy on the heart but can leave you chilled in cold weather, so dress for it, watch for traffic when you stop, build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Concept: Stop for Anything. A run where you must stop for anything interesting (a dog, a strange door, a bird) and look as long as you like. Score the run in stops, not kilometers. Swapping achievement for curiosity for an hour.

modalities.name: Carry One Question
modalities.tagline: Take one question on a hard solo run, and see what comes.
modalities.whatItIs: Carry One Question is a solo running practice that pairs hard effort with a single question you take along, such as a decision or a puzzle. Animal-assisted therapy offers calm company and attention turned outward. This is the opposite, alone, effortful and inward: part physical challenge, part private thinking space.
modalities.coreIdea: A hard run with one question in mind gives the mind room to turn it over while the body is busy, and some people find it looks different afterward.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before you go, you write one question on a card, such as 'what do I want from this job?', and leave it at home. You run for 30 to 50 minutes alone at a hard, steady pace, coming back to the question whenever your mind wanders. When you get home, you spend five minutes writing down whatever came up.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who think better on the move, and anyone stuck on a decision who wants a different way to approach it.
modalities.cautions: Being lost in thought on a hard run makes you less alert to traffic and terrain, so use safe, familiar routes, build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, and big personal decisions may still need talking through with someone you trust or a professional.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Carry One Question. Write one question on a card, leave it at home, then go for a hard solo run and let your mind turn it over. Write down what came up when you get back. Made for people who think best when their legs are busy.

modalities.name: Summit Shout
modalities.tagline: Run hard up every hill and shout at the top.
modalities.whatItIs: Summit Shout is a hard hill run with a loud ending to every climb: at the top of each hill, if nobody is close by, you let out one full shout, as loud as you like. Qigong regulates the breath quietly and keeps energy contained. This spends it, out loud.
modalities.coreIdea: A full-voiced shout after hard effort may give pent-up tension a way out that daily life rarely allows.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two or three times a week you run a 30 to 45 minute route with three to six climbs, pushing steadily up each one. At the top, after checking that nobody nearby will be startled, you shout one long sound or word, then jog easily down. Some people choose a word for the day, others just roar.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who hold a lot in, rarely raise their voice, or carry tension they cannot name.
modalities.cautions: Hard climbs strain the heart and legs, so build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems; shout only where it will not alarm anyone, and stop if your voice gets hoarse. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Hypothetical practice: Summit Shout. Run hard up every hill and, at the top, if nobody's close, let out one full-voiced shout. Then jog down and do it again. Somewhere to put everything you hold in all week. ⛰️

modalities.name: Stash for Yourself
modalities.tagline: Hide water and a note halfway, then run to it.
modalities.whatItIs: Stash for Yourself is a hard, solo run with a gift waiting halfway: before you set out, you hide a bottle of water and a note to yourself somewhere along the route, then you run to it, read it and run home. You are your own support crew, with nobody else involved.
modalities.coreIdea: Preparing something kind for your later self, then receiving it mid-effort, may be practice in looking after yourself the way you would look after someone else.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week you walk or cycle part of your route beforehand and leave water and a short note (an encouragement, a joke or a reminder) in a safe, discreet spot. Later you run for 40 to 60 minutes at a hard, steady effort, collect the stash at the halfway point and read the note before heading home. You take everything back with you.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who look after everyone except themselves, and runners who train alone and would like a small moment of support.
modalities.cautions: Hard solo runs strain the heart and muscles and nobody is there if something goes wrong, so tell someone your route, carry a phone, leave nothing behind, build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Stash for Yourself. Before a hard solo run, hide water and a note to yourself halfway along the route. Later you run to it, drink, read what you wrote and run home. Being your own support crew for once.

modalities.name: Lamppost Vocabulary
modalities.tagline: Recall one word of a new language at every lamppost.
modalities.whatItIs: Lamppost Vocabulary turns a hard, steady run along lit streets into a language lesson: you carry a short list of words in a language you are learning and test yourself on one at each lamppost. The route is a grid of streets rather than open countryside, and the mind gets a small, absorbing job. That puts it on the far side of running from a nature walk's open, drifting attention.
modalities.coreIdea: Giving a busy or worried mind a small learning game to play while the body works may crowd out rumination and leave you with something gained.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you run for 25 to 40 minutes along lit streets, with ten new words on a card in your pocket. At each lamppost you recall one word's meaning, checking the card only at junctions, and on the way back you test yourself in reverse. At home you mark the words you knew.
modalities.whoItsFor: People learning a language, and anyone whose mind loops on worries when it has nothing to do.
modalities.cautions: Thinking hard while running makes you less alert to traffic, so use quiet streets with pavements, look up at every crossing, build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Idea: Lamppost Vocabulary. Run with ten words of a language you're learning and recall one at every lamppost, then test yourself in reverse on the way home. A small game for a mind that loops when it has nothing to do.

modalities.name: Invented Kingdom Route
modalities.tagline: Turn your dullest route into a world only you know.
modalities.whatItIs: Invented Kingdom Route turns a dull, familiar run into an imagined world: each landmark becomes a place in a story you build over weeks, so the bus stop is a border post and the hill is a mountain pass. Sensory mindfulness anchors attention in what is really there, while here imagination takes over the route. The running is hard and steady, and the story is yours.
modalities.coreIdea: Building a private imagined world along a real route may make a dull run something to look forward to and give the imagination a playful outlet.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two or three times a week you run the same 30 to 50 minute route, and each time you add to the story: name a new place, invent who lives there, decide what happens on the climb. After the run you add one line to a notebook map of the kingdom. Over months the route becomes a world only you know.
modalities.whoItsFor: Imaginative people bored by running, and anyone who wants some play back in their week.
modalities.cautions: Daydreaming makes you less alert to traffic and terrain, so use safe, familiar routes, build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Imagine your dullest running route as a kingdom: the bus stop is a border post, the hill a mountain pass. Invented Kingdom Route adds a little story every run, until after a few months your route is a world only you know.

modalities.name: Thanks Per Kilometer
modalities.tagline: Every kilometer, name one thing from your day that went right.
modalities.whatItIs: Thanks Per Kilometer is a hard, steady solo run in which every kilometer marker, or every five minutes, is a cue to name one specific thing from your day that went right, silently or under your breath. There is no music and no audio, just the run and a list growing in your head. Music stirs feelings from outside, and this asks you to find a good one yourself, again and again.
modalities.coreIdea: Naming a specific good thing at each kilometer may tilt attention toward what went right, especially on days that felt as if nothing did.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you run for 30 to 50 minutes and, at each kilometer, name one specific thing from the last day, however small, such as 'the bus was on time' or 'she laughed at my joke'. No repeats are allowed within a run. Back home you can write the list down or let it go.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who end the day remembering only what went wrong, and runners who want a run to leave them with more than tired legs.
modalities.cautions: Hard running carries injury and heart strain risks, so build up gradually and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems. It is an untested idea, and it should never become a way to deny real problems that need attention.
modalities.tweet: Concept: Thanks Per Kilometer. On a hard solo run, at every kilometer, name one specific thing from your day that went right ('the bus was on time'). No repeats. By the end you've run a list your tired brain would never have made on its own.

modalities.name: The Can-Do List
modalities.tagline: Track only what your body can do, never how it looks.
modalities.whatItIs: The Can-Do List is strength training whose only record is a list of things your body can now do: carry both shopping bags up the stairs, get up off the floor without hands, do ten clean push-ups. There are no photos, no measurements and no mirror checks, and you set up every lift facing a wall or window. The program itself is strict and self-run.
modalities.coreIdea: Measuring strength only by new abilities may shift attention from how the body looks to what it lets you do in daily life.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you follow a written plan of five or six lifts, and after each session you ask whether there is anything you can now do that you could not before. When there is, you add it to the list in plain words, such as 'lifted the full suitcase into the car'. Once a month you read the whole list from the top.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel self-conscious or critical about their bodies, and anyone who wants strength to be about what they can do, not how they look.
modalities.cautions: Without a mirror you lose some feedback on form, so learn the lifts from a qualified coach first, use safety bars or a spotter on squats and presses, keep loads moderate and avoid holding your breath; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea, and strong body image worries call for professional help.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: The Can-Do List. Strength training where the only record is a list of things your body can now do ('carried the suitcase upstairs', 'got up off the floor without hands'). No photos, no mirror checks. Strength measured in life, not looks.

modalities.name: Strong in Every Room
modalities.tagline: One hard set in every place in your life, every week.
modalities.whatItIs: Strong in Every Room takes one short, hard strength set out of the gym and into each place in your life: squats in the kitchen, push-ups in the office stairwell, a lift with a full laundry basket at home. The gym program stays strict, but over a week the same strong self turns up everywhere.
modalities.coreIdea: Putting the same hard effort into every room of your life may make the capable you feel like who you are, not someone who exists only at the gym.
modalities.whatYouDo: Alongside two or three normal gym sessions a week, you pick five places (kitchen, desk, hallway, park, a friend's house) and do one hard set of a body-weight or household-object lift in each during the week. You tick each place off on a small card. Every month you add a new room.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel like a different person at work, at home and with friends, and anyone whose confidence stays behind at the gym.
modalities.cautions: Household objects are awkward to lift, so keep them light and stable, use good form and avoid holding your breath, and in the gym use safety bars for heavy lifts; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: What if your strength didn't stay at the gym? Strong in Every Room: one hard set in each place in your life (kitchen squats, stairwell push-ups, a laundry-basket lift) until the strong version of you shows up everywhere. An untested idea.

modalities.name: Covered Plates
modalities.tagline: A partner loads the bar; you never learn the number.
modalities.whatItIs: Covered Plates is strength training in which you never learn how much you are lifting: a training partner loads the bar or picks the dumbbells, and the numbers stay covered with tape. You lift what is in front of you as well as you can, judged by feel and form. Nothing is recorded by you, which puts it at the far end from the thought records and worksheets of CBT.
modalities.coreIdea: Lifting without knowing the number may loosen its grip, so a lift is judged by how it moved rather than by what it seems to say about you.
modalities.whatYouDo: Twice a week a partner who knows your rough working weights loads each set within an agreed safe range and keeps a private log. You do your sets and say only 'heavier', 'same' or 'lighter' for next time. Once a month the partner shows you the log, and you notice how it feels to see the numbers again.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose mood rises and falls with numbers, on the bar, the scale or a screen, and lifters who have stopped enjoying lifting.
modalities.cautions: Not knowing the load means trusting your partner, so agree a safe range in advance, use safety bars or a spotter on squats and bench presses, stop any set that feels wrong and avoid holding your breath; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Covered Plates. A partner loads the bar and tapes over the numbers, so you never know what you're lifting. You just lift it well and say 'heavier', 'same' or 'lighter'. Strength training with the number taken away.

modalities.name: Spiral Breaker Squats
modalities.tagline: Catch a thought spiral, do one hard set right there.
modalities.whatItIs: Spiral Breaker Squats is a strength habit built as an interrupt: whenever you notice your thoughts spiraling, you stand up and do one hard set of squats or push-ups wherever you are, then carry on. A normal structured strength plan runs alongside it, so that those sets are strong and safe. ACT teaches making room for thoughts, and this works the other way, changing state through the body.
modalities.coreIdea: A short, hard burst of effort the moment you notice a spiral may break its momentum and leave a clear moment to choose what to do next.
modalities.whatYouDo: Twice a week you do a 40-minute strength session to build the movements, and the rest of the time you keep one rule: when you catch yourself spiraling, do 10 to 15 squats or push-ups at once, as well as you can. Afterward you take one breath and choose your next action. You tally the interrupts on your phone for a month.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who ruminate or go round in circles of thought, and anyone who wants a physical way to step out of a spiral.
modalities.cautions: Sudden hard sets without a warm-up can strain muscles, so keep them moderate, use good form and avoid holding your breath, and in the gym use safety bars for heavy lifts; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea and no substitute for help if rumination or low mood persists.
modalities.tweet: Idea: Spiral Breaker Squats. When you catch your thoughts spiraling, stand up and do one hard set of squats or push-ups right where you are, take one breath, then choose your next move. A physical interrupt for a looping mind.

modalities.name: Two-Choice Sets
modalities.tagline: Two safe options before every set, five seconds to choose.
modalities.whatItIs: Two-Choice Sets is a strength session in which every set begins with a small, fast decision: you have two safe options, such as heavier or more reps, and must choose within five seconds, then commit fully. The plan around those choices is strict and written in advance.
modalities.coreIdea: Making many small choices quickly, and finding that most of them turn out fine, may ease the paralysis of needing the perfect decision.
modalities.whatYouDo: You write a plan of five lifts in which each set lists two safe options, such as '8 reps at your usual weight, or 5 reps slightly heavier'. Before each set you count to five out loud and choose, with no switching afterward. After the session you note which choices you would make again, and how few of them mattered much.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who agonize over small decisions, and lifters who stall while planning every detail.
modalities.cautions: Both options on every card must be within your safe range, so write them in advance with a coach's help if you are new, use safety bars or a spotter on squats and presses and avoid holding your breath; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Speculative idea: Two-Choice Sets. Before every set you get two safe options (heavier, or more reps) and five seconds to choose. No switching. A strength session that doubles as practice in small, fast decisions, for people who agonize over every one.

modalities.name: Eyes Closed Bodyweight
modalities.tagline: Hard body-weight sets with your eyes shut, a rail within reach.
modalities.whatItIs: Eyes Closed Bodyweight is a structured session of hard body-weight moves, such as split squats beside a rail, wall push-ups and step-ups, done with your eyes closed. Without sight you have to feel where your body is, through your feet, joints and balance. TRE lets the body shake involuntarily; this is deliberate, controlled effort guided only by your inner sense of position.
modalities.coreIdea: Working hard and moving well with your eyes closed may build trust in your body's own sense of where it is, for people who feel clumsy or cut off from it.
modalities.whatYouDo: Twice a week you do five body-weight exercises next to a wall or a sturdy rail, first with eyes open, then with eyes closed, for 2 or 3 sets of 8 to 12 slow reps that end close to your limit. After each set you open your eyes and check your position. Over the weeks you rely less and less on the support.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel disconnected from their body or clumsy, and anyone who wants to trust their body more.
modalities.cautions: Closing your eyes affects balance, so always stay within reach of a wall or rail, clear the space around you, never use weights with your eyes closed, keep breathing rather than holding your breath and stop if you feel dizzy; people with balance problems, recent falls, uncontrolled high blood pressure or heart problems should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: New idea: Eyes Closed Bodyweight. Hard sets of split squats, wall push-ups and step-ups done with your eyes shut and a hand near a rail, feeling where your body is instead of watching it. Building trust in your own sense of position.

modalities.name: Anger Gets One Set
modalities.tagline: When anger hits, it gets one planned, safe, hard set.
modalities.whatItIs: Anger Gets One Set gives anger a structured, physical outlet: when you are angry, instead of reacting, you do one planned, hard set of a safe exercise at a moderate weight, then decide what to do about the situation. The rest of your training follows a normal strict plan.
modalities.coreIdea: Having a planned, safe place to put the energy of anger may create a pause between feeling it and acting on it.
modalities.whatYouDo: You choose one 'anger set' in advance, such as 15 goblet squats with a moderate kettlebell or a hard minute of push-ups, and practice it in normal sessions. When anger rises, you do that set, breathing out on every rep, then sit for one minute before deciding your next step. You note what you decided and whether it still seems right the next day.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who snap, say things they regret or bottle anger up, and who want a structured option somewhere in between.
modalities.cautions: Strong emotion makes people lift carelessly, so the anger set must use a moderate weight you know well, never maximal loads or a barbell without safety bars, and you should keep breathing rather than hold your breath; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea, and anger that feels out of control or leads to harm needs professional help.
modalities.tweet: Concept: Anger Gets One Set. Pick one safe, hard set in advance (15 squats with a moderate kettlebell). When anger hits, do the set, breathe out on every rep, sit for a minute, then decide what to do. A planned place to put the energy.

modalities.name: One Proud Sentence
modalities.tagline: End every session by saying one true thing you did well.
modalities.whatItIs: One Proud Sentence ends every strength session with a rule: before you leave, you say out loud one specific thing you did well, starting with 'I'm proud that...'. The program before it is structured and self-run, and the sentence is the part that never gets skipped.
modalities.coreIdea: Saying a specific achievement out loud, every session, may make it easier to notice and own your progress instead of brushing it aside.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you follow a written plan of five lifts, using safety bars on squats and presses. At the end you stand still and say one sentence aloud, such as 'I'm proud that I kept my form on the last set', and it has to be specific and true. You write each sentence on the back of your plan, so after a few months you have a page of them.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who downplay their achievements, deflect praise or never feel they have done enough.
modalities.cautions: Pride can tempt people to chase bigger numbers, so add weight gradually, use safety bars or a spotter for heavy lifts and avoid holding your breath; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Proposal: One Proud Sentence. End every strength session by saying out loud one specific, true thing you did well ('I'm proud that I kept my form on the last set'). Then write it down. A page of them, months later, is hard to argue with.

modalities.name: Fact After Every Set
modalities.tagline: After each set, one plain fact before any verdict.
