modalities.whatItIs: Fact After Every Set is a strict strength program with one extra step: after each set, you say one plain, neutral fact about it ('eight reps, the last two slow') before any judgment creeps in. No 'good', no 'bad', no 'pathetic', only what happened. Where Do Nothing meditation lets the mind do whatever it does, this deliberately steers it toward plain description, set after set.
modalities.coreIdea: Describing your effort in plain facts instead of verdicts, many times a session, may weaken the habit of harsh self-judgment.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you follow a structured plan of five or six lifts, with safety bars or a spotter on heavy squats and presses. After each set you say or write one factual sentence, and if a judgment slips in, you rephrase it as a fact. Once a week you read back the facts and see what they actually show.
modalities.whoItsFor: People with a harsh inner critic, and lifters who call every set either great or terrible.
modalities.cautions: Heavy sets are risky without good technique, so learn the lifts from a qualified coach, use safety bars or a spotter, add weight gradually and avoid holding your breath; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea and no replacement for therapy if self-criticism is severe.
modalities.tweet: Idea: Fact After Every Set. After each set, say one plain fact about it ('eight reps, last two slow') before any verdict sneaks in. No 'good', no 'pathetic', just what happened. Practice in describing yourself without judging yourself.

modalities.name: Mood-Proof Training
modalities.tagline: Train at fixed times, whatever you feel like.
modalities.whatItIs: Mood-Proof Training is strength training booked at fixed times and done whether or not you feel motivated. Metta and jhana practice cultivate a feeling first; here action comes first and does not wait for any feeling at all. The plan is strict, and your mood is welcome but has no vote.
modalities.coreIdea: Acting first and letting feelings follow, or not, may loosen the link between how you feel and what you do.
modalities.whatYouDo: You book three 40-minute sessions a week at fixed times, like appointments, and follow a written plan. On low-motivation days the only rule is to start: do the warm-up and the first set, then decide whether to continue, with a lighter version always allowed. You track attendance, not performance.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who wait to feel ready before acting, and anyone whose exercise habit collapses when motivation dips.
modalities.cautions: Training through every mood must never mean training through pain, illness or exhaustion, so rest when unwell, use the lighter version freely, use safety bars or a spotter for heavy lifts and avoid holding your breath; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure or heart problems should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea, and persistent low mood deserves a conversation with a doctor.
modalities.tweet: Idea: Mood-Proof Training. Book three strength sessions a week like appointments. On low days the only rule is to start: warm up, do one set, then decide. Track showing up, not performance. For anyone who waits to feel ready before doing anything.

modalities.name: Rush Hour Gym
modalities.tagline: Train at the gym's busiest hour, on purpose.
modalities.whatItIs: Rush Hour Gym is strength training done deliberately at the busiest time in a public gym, when the benches are taken and people are all around. You follow a strict plan and practice staying with your own training while strangers watch, wait and pass. Vipassana is learned in silence and solitude, and this happens in the middle of a crowd.
modalities.coreIdea: Training steadily among many strangers, week after week, may make being seen in public feel more ordinary for people who dread it.
modalities.whatYouDo: Twice a week you go at the gym's peak hour with a written plan of four or five lifts and a backup exercise for each in case equipment is busy. You ask to share equipment at least once per session and notice how it actually goes compared with what you feared. You note one moment each session that was easier than expected.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who avoid gyms because of other people, feel watched or judged, or only train when the place is empty.
modalities.cautions: Crowded gyms mean tight spaces and rushed sets, so give yourself room, use safety bars or ask staff to spot heavy lifts and avoid holding your breath; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea, and strong social anxiety is treatable, so talk to a doctor or therapist rather than pushing through alone.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Rush Hour Gym. Go to the gym at its busiest, on purpose, with a plan and a backup for every exercise, and ask to share a bench at least once. Week by week, being seen while you train becomes ordinary.

modalities.name: Evening Wind-Down Sets
modalities.tagline: Twenty unhurried minutes of strength that close the day.
modalities.whatItIs: Evening Wind-Down Sets is a slow, calm strength routine done in the evening to close the day: a few moderate lifts at an unhurried pace, long exhales between reps, dimmed light and no screens. The routine is fixed and short, and it never leaves you breathless.
modalities.coreIdea: A short, steady effort followed by slowing down may give the day a clear ending and a feeling of being strong and calm at the same time.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three evenings a week, at least an hour before bed, you do four moderate exercises, such as slow split squats, dumbbell rows and glute bridges, for 2 sets of 8 at about 6 out of 10 effort. Between sets you breathe out slowly and lower the lights a little more each time. The routine takes 20 minutes and ends with two minutes of sitting still.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who struggle to switch off in the evening, and anyone who wants a calm way to fit strength into their week.
modalities.cautions: Exercise close to bedtime keeps some people awake, so finish at least an hour before sleep and stop if it does; keep loads moderate, use good form and avoid holding your breath, and get medical advice first if you have uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease. It is an untested idea and not a substitute for help with sleep problems.
modalities.tweet: An idea for restless evenings: Evening Wind-Down Sets. Twenty unhurried minutes of moderate lifts, long exhales between reps, the lights dimmed a little after every set, then two minutes of sitting still. Ending the day strong and settled.

modalities.name: Floor Rests
modalities.tagline: Between hard sets, lie flat and let everything go heavy.
modalities.whatItIs: Floor Rests is solo strength training in which every rest period is spent lying flat on the floor, eyes closed, letting the body go completely heavy before the next hard set. The program is strict and done alone, without music or phone.
modalities.coreIdea: Alternating real effort with real surrender may make it easier to let go fully once the work is done, for people who never stop bracing.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you do four or five lifts for 3 sets of 5 to 8 reps, with safety bars where needed. After each set you lie on a mat for two to three minutes, feel your heartbeat slow and let your shoulders, jaw and hands soften, then stand up slowly for the next set. Sessions take about an hour.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who stay tense even when resting, and anyone who finds it hard to stop once they start.
modalities.cautions: Getting up quickly after lying down can make you dizzy, so rise slowly, keep breathing during lifts rather than holding your breath and use safety bars or a spotter for heavy lifts; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Floor Rests. Hard solo strength sets, and between every one, two minutes lying flat on the floor, eyes closed, letting your whole body go heavy. Practice in working hard and then really letting go, again and again.

modalities.name: Five Single Reps
modalities.tagline: Five separate reps, each one finished before the next.
modalities.whatItIs: Five Single Reps is a very short strength session made of five separate repetitions, each a complete act: set up, one careful rep, set the weight down, step away and reset. Nothing runs into anything else.
modalities.coreIdea: Doing one thing completely before starting the next, five times in a row, may be a small antidote to a day spent half-doing many things at once.
modalities.whatYouDo: A qualified coach teaches you one lift, such as a trap-bar deadlift or a goblet squat, and picks a moderate weight you can lift cleanly. Three times a week you do five single reps, each followed by setting the weight down, walking away and a full minute of stillness, with safety bars or pins for any barbell lift. The session takes about ten minutes.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who multitask all day and rarely finish anything fully, and anyone who wants a very short, very focused session.
modalities.cautions: Single reps tempt people to go heavy, so keep the weight moderate, learn the lift from a coach, use safety bars or pins and breathe rather than hold your breath; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Concept: Five Single Reps. Five separate reps, each one complete: set up, lift once, set it down, walk away, a minute of stillness. Ten minutes of doing one thing fully before starting the next, after a day of half-doing everything.

modalities.name: Hand on Heart Finish
modalities.tagline: After the hardest set, a hand on your chest, one kind sentence.
modalities.whatItIs: Hand on Heart Finish is a hard, solo strength program with one ritual: right after the hardest set of every session, you put a hand flat on your chest, feel your heart pounding and say one kind sentence to yourself. Animal-assisted therapy brings comfort from another living being. Here, alone and still breathing hard, you practice giving it to yourself.
modalities.coreIdea: Offering yourself a kind word at the moment you are most strained may make self-kindness feel less awkward and more natural.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you follow a written plan of five lifts, with safety bars or a spotter on heavy squats and presses. After the last, hardest set you sit or stand, place a hand on your chest for 30 seconds and say one sentence such as 'that was hard, and you did it'. You keep the sentence simple and the same for a few weeks.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are hard on themselves, especially when tired or struggling, and anyone who finds self-kindness embarrassing.
modalities.cautions: Hard sets raise blood pressure, especially with breath-holding, so keep breathing, use safety bars or a spotter, add weight gradually and get medical advice first if you have uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease. It is an untested idea, and the kind words must never become a reason to ignore pain.
modalities.tweet: New idea: Hand on Heart Finish. After the hardest set of your workout, put a hand on your pounding chest and say one kind sentence to yourself ('that was hard, and you did it'). Self-kindness practiced at the moment it's hardest to offer.

modalities.name: Weekly Load Set Down
modalities.tagline: Load the week into a sandbag, lift it, set it down.
modalities.whatItIs: Weekly Load Set Down is a vigorous end-of-week strength ritual: you write each thing weighing on you this week (a task, a decision, a worry) on a card, put the cards in a sandbag or backpack with the training weight, work through a hard circuit with it, then set it down, take the cards out and throw them away. Qigong cultivates calm, slow, inner energy. This is loud, effortful and very literal.
modalities.coreIdea: Making the week's load physically heavy for a while and then deliberately putting it down may give the end of a week a concrete, bodily shape.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week you add the cards to a sandbag or backpack loaded with a moderate, known weight and do a structured circuit with it, such as 5 rounds of 10 squats, a 30-meter carry and 10 bent-over rows. Then you set it down with care, take out the cards and bin or shred them. You note any card that needs a real action and plan that separately.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who carry the week around with them into the weekend, and anyone who likes a physical, symbolic way to mark an ending.
modalities.cautions: Loaded bags shift and strain the back, so keep the weight moderate, keep your back neutral, breathe rather than hold your breath and set the load down with control; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea, and real problems still need real steps, not only a ritual.
modalities.tweet: Experimental ritual: Weekly Load Set Down. Write what's weighing on you on cards, load them into the sandbag, lift and carry it through a hard circuit, then set it down, pull the cards out and bin them. The end of the week, made heavy and then put down.

modalities.name: Unreachable Hour
modalities.tagline: Tell people you're unreachable, lock the phone away, lift.
modalities.whatItIs: Unreachable Hour is a strict, solo strength session that starts with telling the people around you that you will be unreachable for an hour, then putting your phone in a locker or another room. A coach writes the program, and you follow it alone and in silence.
modalities.coreIdea: Announcing an hour of being unreachable, and finding that the world copes, may make it easier to protect time for yourself.
modalities.whatYouDo: Twice a week you send a short message such as 'training, back at 7', put the phone away and work through a coach-written plan of five or six lifts, using safety bars or pins for heavy squats and presses. Afterward, before checking the phone, you note what you expect to have missed. Then you check and compare.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel they must always answer, such as carers, managers and parents, and anyone who cannot protect an hour for themselves.
modalities.cautions: Training alone means nobody can help if something goes wrong, so use safety bars or pins, stay below your limit, keep breathing rather than holding your breath and make sure someone knows where you are; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea, and it is not for times when someone genuinely depends on reaching you.
modalities.tweet: Idea: Unreachable Hour. Text 'training, back at 7', lock the phone away and lift alone for an hour. Before you check it, guess what you missed, then compare. Usually the world coped. Protecting one hour for yourself, twice a week.

modalities.name: Sealed Envelope Sessions
modalities.tagline: Each workout sealed in an envelope, opened only at the gym.
modalities.whatItIs: Sealed Envelope Sessions is strength training in which a coach writes eight weeks of sessions and seals each in a numbered envelope, which you open only when you arrive to train. You cannot plan ahead, change the order or peek. A nature walk is open, unplanned wandering, and this is the reverse, tightly structured, except that the structure belongs to someone else and arrives as a surprise.
modalities.coreIdea: Committing to a plan you cannot see, written by someone you trust, may be practice in tolerating not knowing what comes next.
modalities.whatYouDo: A qualified coach assesses you in one session and writes 16 to 24 sessions within loads you can safely handle, each in its own envelope. Two or three times a week you open the next one at the gym and do exactly what it says, using safety bars or a spotter for heavy lifts. After each session you write one line on how it felt not to know.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who need to plan and control everything, and anyone who struggles with uncertainty.
modalities.cautions: Surprise sessions only stay safe if the coach knows your health and limits, so be open with them, skip any exercise that causes pain, use safety bars or a spotter and avoid holding your breath; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea, and anxiety about uncertainty that runs your life deserves professional help.
modalities.tweet: Hypothetical program: Sealed Envelope Sessions. A coach writes eight weeks of workouts and seals each in an envelope. You open the next one only when you arrive at the gym. No peeking, no planning ahead. Practice in not knowing what comes next. ✉️

modalities.name: Explain Every Rep
modalities.tagline: Narrate each lift out loud as if teaching a beginner.
modalities.whatItIs: Explain Every Rep is strength training in which you narrate each lift out loud as if teaching it to a beginner: where your feet go, what you brace, why the bar moves the way it does. The program itself is structured and demanding.
modalities.coreIdea: Explaining what you are doing as if you were the expert may build a sense of competence and help you take your own knowledge seriously.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you follow a written plan of five lifts, explaining each lift aloud before and between the reps of its first set, quietly if others are near, or into a voice note at home. Every few weeks you teach one lift to a friend for real. You notice which parts you cannot yet explain and look them up.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who doubt their own competence or feel like impostors, and lifters who want to understand their technique better.
modalities.cautions: Talking during a lift can make you hold or lose your breath, so explain between reps rather than under heavy load, use safety bars or a spotter and add weight gradually; people with uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease should get medical advice first. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Explain Every Rep. Narrate each lift out loud as if teaching a beginner: feet, brace, bar path, why. Every few weeks, teach it to a friend for real. Strength training for people who feel like impostors in what they already know.

modalities.name: Calm Face Under Load
modalities.tagline: Keep a soft, calm face through your hardest reps.
modalities.whatItIs: Calm Face Under Load is strength training in which you keep your face soft and neutral through the hardest reps: no grimace, no clenched jaw, eyes calm, even when the effort is close to your limit. The program is structured and done alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Keeping a calm face under real strain may be practice in composure, and some people find that softening the face also eases the sense of struggle.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week you follow a plan of five lifts, and on the last two reps of each set you check your jaw, brow and hands and soften them while keeping your brace and form. A phone propped up to film your face, not your body, shows you how it went. Over time you try the same soft face in stressful moments outside the gym.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose stress shows in their face or jaw, and anyone who wants practice staying composed under pressure.
modalities.cautions: Relaxing the face must never mean relaxing your brace or form, and you should keep breathing rather than hold your breath; use safety bars or a spotter for heavy lifts and get medical advice first if you have uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: What if you could lift your hardest set with a calm face? Calm Face Under Load: soft jaw, easy brow, quiet eyes on the last two reps, brace and form unchanged. An untested idea for practicing composure where it's hardest to keep.
